practice_questions.text: Name the marking-out tool used to make a small indent in metal before drilling.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: centre punch. No other answer accepted.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between a hacksaw and a bandsaw.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each (max 2) for any two from: hacksaw is a hand tool / bandsaw is powered; hacksaw has a straight blade in a frame / bandsaw has a continuous loop blade; hacksaw is slower / bandsaw cuts faster; bandsaw can cut curves / hacksaw is used for straight cuts primarily. Accept other valid engineering distinctions.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of marking out a hole position on a metal plate before drilling.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes using a scriber to mark the centre position from the drawing; using a centre punch and hammer to create an indent at the marked point; checking the position against the drawing using a steel rule or vernier caliper. Secure: Mentions scriber and centre punch but omits the purpose of the centre punch indent. Developing: Mentions one tool with a brief description. Emerging: States 'mark the position' without naming tools.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a workpiece must always be clamped to the pillar drill table rather than held by hand during drilling.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that if the drill bit snags or breaks through the material suddenly, the workpiece will spin with considerable force, causing serious injury to the operator; clamping prevents this rotation; also notes that hand-holding provides no control over the position of the cut, reducing accuracy. Secure: Explains the snagging/spinning injury risk clearly; may not mention the accuracy point. Developing: States it is safer without explaining the mechanism of injury. Emerging: States to clamp without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a centre lathe and a milling machine, and give one engineering task that each is better suited for.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that on a lathe the workpiece rotates and the tool is fixed, making it suited for cylindrical shapes and thread cutting; on a milling machine the cutter rotates and the workpiece moves, making it suited for flat surfaces, slots and profiled edges. Gives one appropriate task for each. Secure: Explains the rotation difference correctly for both machines; gives one suitable task for each. Developing: Correctly describes one machine but confuses which part rotates on the other. Emerging: Names both machines without distinguishing how they work.

practice_questions.text: A student is asked to produce a mild steel bracket. The bracket requires a straight cut along its length, two holes of different diameters, and one flat machined surface. Describe the sequence of processes and tools that should be used to produce the bracket.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes a logical sequence: mark out dimensions using scriber and try-square; centre punch hole positions; cut to length with hacksaw; file cut edge smooth and de-burr; drill holes on pillar drill (clamped, correct speeds for each diameter); machine flat surface on milling machine or use file. Names tools at each stage. Mentions at least one safety consideration. Secure: Describes the main steps in a logical order with most tools named; may omit safety point or one tool name. Developing: Identifies the main processes but not all tools; sequence may have minor logic errors. Emerging: Lists two or three processes without a logical sequence or tool names.

practice_questions.text: A 9 V battery is connected to a resistor of 3 Ω. Calculate the current flowing through the resistor. Show all your working and state the unit.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Formula stated (V = IR or rearrangement), correct substitution (I = 9/3), correct answer 3 A with unit. All four steps present.
Secure: Correct method and answer but unit missing, or minor arithmetic slip with correct method shown.
Developing: Correct formula identified but substitution error, or answer given without working.
Emerging: Relevant formula attempted but no correct answer reached.

practice_questions.text: An electric motor runs from a 24 V supply and has a resistance of 4 Ω. Calculate the power consumed by the motor. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies appropriate power formula (e.g. P = V²/R or finds I first then P = IV), substitutes correctly, reaches P = 144 W with unit.
Secure: Correct method but arithmetic error or unit omitted.
Developing: Identifies a relevant formula but substitution incomplete or incorrect.
Emerging: Recalls a relevant term (power, resistance, voltage) but cannot complete the calculation.

practice_questions.text:
A lever is used to lift a heavy engine block. The load is 900 N and the effort applied is 300 N. The effort moves 1.5 m and the load moves 0.5 m.
(a) Calculate the mechanical advantage of the lever.
(b) Calculate the velocity ratio of the lever.
(c) Calculate the efficiency of the lever. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three parts correct — MA = 3, VR = 3, efficiency = 100% (ideal lever). Units handled correctly (MA and VR dimensionless, efficiency as %).
Secure: Two of the three parts fully correct, or all three correct with a method error in one step.
Developing: One part fully correct, or correct formulae stated but substitution errors present.
Emerging: At least one relevant formula identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the efficiency of a real lever is always less than 100%, even when it has been precisely machined. Use your knowledge of energy to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States real machines lose energy to friction at the pivot; this wasted energy appears as heat; therefore output energy (useful work) is always less than input energy; hence MA < VR and efficiency < 100%.
Secure: Links friction/energy loss to efficiency below 100% with one clear developed reason.
Developing: States friction reduces efficiency but does not explain the energy relationship.
Emerging: States a real machine is not perfect without further development.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between mechanical advantage and velocity ratio.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Mechanical advantage is a ratio of forces (Load ÷ Effort).
1 mark: Velocity ratio is a ratio of distances (distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load). Do not accept answers that confuse the two.

practice_questions.text: A trolley jack in a car workshop has a mechanical advantage of 6 and a velocity ratio of 8. Discuss whether this machine is well designed for its purpose, considering both its efficiency and its practical usefulness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculates efficiency (75%); comments that 75% is reasonably high for a hydraulic jack with friction losses; identifies that MA of 6 is very useful (a mechanic applies 100 N and lifts 600 N of vehicle); notes the trade-off: the handle must move 8 cm for every 1 cm of lift; concludes the design is appropriate because force multiplication is the primary requirement; acknowledges that efficiency could be improved with better seals/lubrication. Sustained, developed argument throughout.
Secure: Calculates efficiency correctly and makes two developed points about practical usefulness or trade-off.
Developing: Calculates efficiency or makes basic points about usefulness without fully developing both strands.
Emerging: States a relevant term (mechanical advantage, efficiency) but does not develop the argument.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the diamond frame geometry used on modern bicycles?
A) A circular arrangement of tubes that spreads load equally in all directions
B) Two triangles sharing a common side, distributing rider weight efficiently
C) A single rectangular tube running from handlebars to rear wheel
D) A curved monocoque shell similar to a car body
practice_questions.marks: B) Two triangles sharing a common side, distributing rider weight efficiently [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the type of engineering design that focuses on the development of theme-park rides.
practice_questions.marks: Mechanical design [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why aluminium alloy became a popular frame material for bicycles, replacing mild steel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct reason, up to 2 marks:
- Lower density / lighter than steel for the same volume
- Good corrosion resistance / does not rust like steel
- Sufficient strength for most cycling applications
(Any two of the above for 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe the development of the rail and wheel system used on modern roller coasters.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark for each distinct point up to 3 marks:
- Early coasters used basic flat rails with wheels running on top, which could leave the track at speed
- Modern coasters use a C-shaped channel where wheels grip the rail on three faces (running surface, outside edge and underside)
- This three-sided grip prevents the car from lifting off the rail, allowing upside-down loops to be used safely
(Other valid engineering points accepted)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of integrated circuits contributed to the transformation of mobile phones into smartphones.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Explains that integrated circuits pack many transistors onto a single chip, reducing size and power consumption, allowing complex functions (GPS, camera, internet) to be included in a pocket-sized device, with development linked to improved performance.
Developing: States that integrated circuits made phones smaller or added new features, with limited explanation of how.
Emerging: Vague reference to technology improving without specific engineering content.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is redesigning a city bicycle for commuters. Discuss how developments in frame materials and frame geometry have contributed to making modern bicycles suitable for everyday urban use. In your answer, consider at least two engineering developments.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more well-developed engineering points, each linking the development (e.g. aluminium alloy, diamond frame) to its engineering benefit (low density reduces rider effort, triangular geometry distributes load without requiring heavy tubes) and applying to the commuter context (light enough to carry upstairs, strong enough to carry panniers).
Secure: Two engineering points with clear explanation of how each contributes to urban cycling suitability.
Developing: One well-developed point or two superficial points with limited engineering reasoning.
Emerging: General statements about bicycles improving over time without specific material or geometry content.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following metals is ferrous?
A) Copper
B) Aluminium
C) Mild steel
D) Brass
practice_questions.marks:
C) Mild steel [1 mark]
(Mild steel contains iron; copper, aluminium and brass are non-ferrous)

practice_questions.text: Name the non-ferrous metal most commonly used for electrical wiring.
practice_questions.marks: Copper [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two properties that make stainless steel suitable for kitchen sinks.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct property up to 2 marks:
- Corrosion resistant / does not rust in wet environments
- Easy to clean / hygienic surface
- Tough and durable / resists impact damage from crockery
- Good appearance / attractive silver finish
(Any two for 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe how tool steel differs from mild steel in terms of composition and properties.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each distinct point up to 3 marks:
- Tool steel has a higher carbon content than mild steel
- Tool steel can be hardened by heat treatment (quenching / rapid cooling)
- The result is a harder, more brittle material that holds a cutting edge, unlike mild steel which is tougher but softer
(Other valid points accepted)

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is choosing a material for a bicycle frame. Explain why aluminium alloy is often preferred over mild steel for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Two developed points linking aluminium's properties (lower density/lighter, corrosion resistant) to bicycle requirements (reduces rider effort, no need for protective paint in outdoor conditions), with engineering reasoning.
Developing: States aluminium is lighter or does not rust, with limited explanation of why this matters for a bicycle.
Emerging: Vague reference to aluminium being a better material without specific property or application reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A teacher is equipping a school engineering workshop with tools and equipment. Explain why tool steel is used for drill bits and cutting tools rather than mild steel. In your answer, refer to the relevant material properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more well-developed points covering hardness (tool steel can be hardened by heat treatment to hold a cutting edge that mild steel cannot maintain), edge retention under repeated use, and the trade-off (tool steel is more brittle so a drill bit that is incorrectly used can snap — mild steel would deform rather than fracture, but would blunt too quickly to be useful as a cutting tool).
Secure: Two engineering points with clear explanation of properties and their relevance to cutting tool performance.
Developing: One developed point or two superficial points without full engineering reasoning.
Emerging: General statements about tool steel being harder without explaining the mechanism or trade-off.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes Bluetooth technology?
A) A long-range wireless standard for connecting to the internet
B) A short-range wireless standard for connecting devices within a room
C) A wired standard used to connect a keyboard to a computer
D) A type of integrated circuit used in smartwatches
practice_questions.marks: B) A short-range wireless standard for connecting devices within a room [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one microelectronic component that has made wearable fitness trackers possible.
practice_questions.marks: Accept any one of the following: accelerometer / heart-rate sensor / integrated circuit (IC) / Bluetooth chip / microprocessor [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which Wi-Fi has changed everyday life in the home.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct point up to 2 marks:
- Removes need for network cables, allowing devices throughout the home to connect to the internet wirelessly
- Enables smart home devices (thermostats, security cameras, appliances) to be controlled remotely
- Allows multiple devices (TV, laptop, phone, tablet) to share one internet connection
(Any two correct points for 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe how voice-activated technology in the home benefits users with limited mobility.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each distinct point up to 3 marks:
- Allows lighting, heating and entertainment to be controlled using only speech
- Removes the need to physically reach or press buttons on appliances
- Provides independence for users who may not be able to operate conventional controls
(Other valid points accepted)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the miniaturisation of integrated circuits has changed what engineers are able to include in a modern smartphone compared with an early mobile handset.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Two developed points linking smaller ICs to specific added functions (e.g. GPS navigation, front and rear cameras, multiple radio chips for 4G/5G and Bluetooth and Wi-Fi) all fitting within a slim pocket-sized casing, with explanation of the engineering mechanism.
Developing: States that miniaturisation made phones smaller or allowed more functions, with limited explanation of how.
Emerging: Vague reference to technology improving without specific engineering content.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is developing a new home security system. Discuss how developments in smart technologies and microelectronic components have made modern home security systems possible.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more well-developed points covering both smart technology (Wi-Fi or Bluetooth enabling remote monitoring, voice-activated alert acknowledgement) and microelectronics (miniaturised camera sensors, motion-detection ICs, integrated processing chips), with engineering reasoning applied to a security context.
Secure: Two developed points with clear explanation of the engineering behind each development and a security product example.
Developing: One well-developed point or two superficial points with limited engineering reasoning.
Emerging: General statements about technology improving security without specific engineering development content.

practice_questions.text: State one difference between soldering and brazing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one from: soldering uses a filler that melts below 450°C / brazing uses a filler that melts above 450°C; soldering is used for electronics / brazing is used for heavier structural joints; soldering uses a soldering iron / brazing uses a gas torch and brazing hearth. Accept equivalent distinctions.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why a manufacturer might use nuts and bolts rather than welding to join the parts of an engine.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each (max 2) for any two from: nuts and bolts are a temporary fixing allowing the engine to be disassembled for maintenance; welding is a permanent fixing that would make repair or replacement of individual components impossible without cutting; bolted joints can be re-torqued to specification; different materials can be bolted together where welding would be difficult. Accept valid engineering reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe how brazing is carried out in a workshop and what happens to the parent metals during the process.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes applying flux to the joint; heating the parts on a brazing hearth with a gas torch until the parent metal reaches the correct temperature; touching the brazing rod to the joint so the filler flows by capillary action; explicitly states that the parent metals do not melt. Secure: Describes the heating and filler flow; may not explicitly state parent metals stay solid. Developing: Describes heating and filler but does not mention flux or that parent metals stay solid. Emerging: States it uses heat and a filler rod without further detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between hardening and tempering as heat treatment processes for steel, and why both steps are usually carried out in sequence.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains hardening (heat steel to correct temperature, quench rapidly in water or oil — produces a hard but brittle structure); explains tempering (reheat to a lower temperature, allow to cool in air — reduces brittleness while retaining much of the hardness); explains that tempering is needed because hardened steel alone is too brittle for most practical applications. Secure: Correctly explains both processes with the consequence of each; may not explain why both are needed in sequence. Developing: Explains one process correctly. Emerging: Names both without explaining the effect of either.

practice_questions.text: Explain why welding produces a stronger joint than brazing, and describe one situation where brazing would be preferred over welding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that in welding the parent metals themselves fuse together, creating a joint as strong as the parent metal itself; in brazing only the filler bonds to the solid parent metal surfaces, so the joint relies on the strength of the filler and the bond to the parent. Gives a valid scenario for brazing preference (e.g. joining dissimilar metals that cannot be welded, working with thinner or more delicate materials, school workshop context without welding equipment, or joining copper pipes where brazing is established practice). Secure: Explains the parent metal melting distinction; gives a plausible brazing scenario without full engineering reasoning. Developing: States welding is stronger without explaining why; names a brazing scenario without explanation. Emerging: States welding is stronger without any explanation.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer produces steel outdoor handrails for a public park. Discuss the finishing processes that should be applied after the handrails have been welded and shaped, explaining why each process is needed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Discusses at least two finishing processes (e.g. grinding/filing weld spatter to produce smooth joints — safety for public use; painting or powder coating to prevent corrosion — outdoor environment, rain and moisture; galvanising as an alternative or additional layer; polishing to remove sharp edges and improve appearance). Explains the environmental degradation risk (UV, rain) without treatment. Discusses the consequence of not finishing (corrosion, rough edges causing injury, poor public appearance). Reaches a conclusion on the most important finishing step and why. Secure: Discusses two processes with explanation; may not address all environmental factors. Developing: Identifies two processes with limited explanation. Emerging: Names one or two processes without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a smart material?
A) Carbon fibre reinforced polymer
B) Nitinol (shape-memory alloy)
C) High-impact polystyrene (HIPS)
D) Urea formaldehyde
practice_questions.marks:
B) Nitinol (shape-memory alloy) [1 mark]
(Nitinol changes shape reversibly in response to a temperature stimulus; CFRP is a composite; HIPS is a thermoplastic; urea formaldehyde is a thermosetting plastic)

practice_questions.text: Name the two parts that make up a composite material.
practice_questions.marks: Matrix and reinforcement [1 mark — must state both for the mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why a manufacturer would choose a thermoplastic rather than a thermosetting plastic for a product that will be recycled at end of life.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct reason up to 2 marks:
- Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be re-moulded/recycled
- Thermosetting plastics have a permanent cross-linked structure that cannot be re-melted
- Thermoplastics retain their properties through multiple heating cycles, making recycling viable
(Any two for 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe how thermochromic pigments work and give one engineering application of this smart material.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each distinct point up to 3 marks:
- Thermochromic pigments contain molecules that rearrange structure at a critical temperature
- This causes them to change colour (below critical temperature: one colour; above: another colour)
- The change is reversible; on cooling the pigment returns to its original colour
Application (any one acceptable): baby bath thermometer, mug revealing an image when filled with hot liquid, packaging indicating temperature abuse
(Award up to 3 marks for description + application)

practice_questions.text: Explain why carbon fibre reinforced polymer is chosen for aircraft structural panels despite being more expensive than aluminium alloy.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Two developed points: CFRP has a higher strength-to-weight ratio than aluminium (lighter for equivalent strength, reducing aircraft mass and fuel consumption); CFRP does not corrode (reducing maintenance burden), with engineering reasoning linking each property to the aircraft application.
Developing: States CFRP is stronger or lighter with limited explanation of why weight saving matters in aerospace.
Emerging: Vague reference to being a better material without specific engineering content.

practice_questions.text: A product designer is selecting a material for a personal protective glove to be used when handling sharp metal components. Discuss whether Kevlar or mild steel mesh would be more suitable, considering the material properties required.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more well-developed points comparing Kevlar (flexible, lightweight, cut-resistant, can be woven into a glove form, does not corrode) with steel mesh (heavy, inflexible, may corrode, does not mould to the hand shape), with engineering reasoning applying specific properties to the protective glove context and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Two developed comparative points with engineering reasoning.
Developing: One developed point comparing the two, or two superficial observations without engineering reasoning.
Emerging: States a preference without properties-based justification.

practice_questions.text: A rectangular sheet of aluminium measures 250 mm by 160 mm. A triangular notch with base 40 mm and height 30 mm is cut from one corner. Calculate the area of aluminium remaining. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculates rectangle area (40 000 mm²), calculates triangle area (600 mm²), subtracts to give 39 400 mm². All steps with units shown.
Secure: Correct method for both shapes but arithmetic error, or correct answer with one unit missing.
Developing: Calculates one shape area correctly; attempt at the second.
Emerging: States a relevant formula.

practice_questions.text: A cylindrical aluminium billet has a diameter of 50 mm and a length of 300 mm. Calculate its volume in mm³. Show your working and state the formula used.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States V = πr²h, identifies r = 25 mm, substitutes correctly, calculates 589 048 mm³ (accept values close to this, e.g. using π = 3.14 gives 589 050 mm³). Unit stated.
Secure: Correct method but uses diameter instead of radius — consequential error carried forward, method marks awarded.
Developing: Formula stated and partially substituted; arithmetic incomplete.
Emerging: Identifies a relevant formula (cylinder or circle area).

practice_questions.text: A component drawing is produced to a scale of 1:20. A feature measures 35 mm on the drawing. Calculate the actual length of the feature in mm, and then convert it to metres.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Actual length = 35 × 20 = 700 mm. Converts to 0.7 m. Both steps shown.
Secure: Correct calculation of actual length in mm but conversion step missing or wrong.
Developing: Scale factor correctly identified (×20 or ×20) but only partially applied.
Emerging: Attempts to use the scale ratio.

practice_questions.text: Explain why all dimensions on an engineering component should be measured from a common datum rather than from the end of the previous measurement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that measuring from a chain of previous marks means each small measurement error adds to the previous one (cumulative error); measuring from a fixed datum means errors remain independent and do not accumulate; therefore the finished component is more accurate and closer to the specified dimensions.
Secure: Mentions cumulative error and links it to the advantage of a fixed datum with some development.
Developing: States that a datum is a reference point and gives one benefit without fully explaining cumulative error.
Emerging: Identifies that a datum is used for measurement.

practice_questions.text: A workshop estimates it will need 120 metal brackets per batch. Each bracket requires approximately 0.48 m of steel strip. Steel strip costs £3.95 per metre. Estimate the total material cost for one batch. Show how you rounded your values.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Reasonable rounding shown — e.g. 120 × 0.5 = 60 m (accept 120 × 0.48 = 57.6 m, rounded to 60 m).
1 mark: Estimated cost shown — e.g. 60 × £4 = £240 (accept values in the range £200–£250 with working shown).

practice_questions.text: A machine tool occupies a floor area of 1.8 m by 0.9 m. A workshop technician needs to draw this machine on a floor plan at a scale of 1:50. Calculate the dimensions the machine should be drawn on the plan, giving your answer in mm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 1.8 m = 1800 mm and 0.9 m = 900 mm; divides by 50 to get 36 mm × 18 mm. Both conversion steps and scale steps shown.
Secure: Correct method but either conversion or scale step has an arithmetic error.
Developing: Identifies that drawing length = real length ÷ 50 but does not complete both dimensions.
Emerging: States the direction of the scale relationship (drawing is smaller for a 1:50 scale).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following plastics can be recycled by re-melting?
A) Urea formaldehyde
B) Silicon (silicone)
C) Acrylic
D) Epoxy resin
practice_questions.marks:
C) Acrylic [1 mark]
(Acrylic is a thermoplastic and re-softens on heating; urea formaldehyde, silicon and epoxy resin are thermosetting plastics with cross-linked structures that cannot be re-melted)

practice_questions.text: Name the term used for the total energy consumed in producing a material, from extraction to finished product.
practice_questions.marks: Embodied energy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why aluminium is considered an environmentally preferable choice over some other metals at end of life.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct point up to 2 marks:
- Aluminium can be recycled repeatedly
- Recycling aluminium requires significantly less energy than producing it from bauxite ore
- Aluminium recycling is economically viable and well established in the UK
(Any two for 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between how a thermoplastic and a thermosetting plastic behave at end of life.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each distinct point up to 3 marks:
- Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be re-moulded and recycled
- Thermosetting plastics have a cross-linked structure that does not re-melt when heated
- Thermosetting plastics therefore cannot be recycled and must go to landfill or incineration
(Other valid points accepted)

practice_questions.text: Explain why a manufacturer designing a new electric kettle should consider the embodied energy of the materials they select.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Two developed points linking high embodied energy to greater environmental cost at production, with reference to recyclability at end of life and how choosing lower-embodied-energy or highly recyclable materials reduces overall impact.
Developing: States that embodied energy affects environmental impact with limited explanation of the mechanism or product application.
Emerging: Vague reference to environmental impact without specific engineering content.

practice_questions.text: A bicycle manufacturer wants to improve the sustainability of their product. Discuss the environmental issues the manufacturer should consider across the full life of the bicycle, from materials selection to end-of-life disposal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Multiple stages of the product lifecycle considered (materials/embodied energy, manufacture waste, transport emissions, use-phase energy, disposal and recycling options for steel, aluminium or composite frame), with trade-offs weighed and a reasoned conclusion about the most significant environmental priority. Engineering vocabulary used precisely.
Secure: At least three lifecycle stages addressed with clear engineering explanation for each.
Developing: Two stages considered with some engineering reasoning, or three stages considered at surface level without development.
Emerging: One stage (typically disposal) discussed without considering others.

practice_questions.text: A quality control team tests 120 components for surface finish. They classify results into four categories: Excellent (48), Good (36), Acceptable (24), Reject (12). Calculate the sector angle for each category and state whether a pie chart or bar chart is more suitable for displaying this data. Justify your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculates all four angles correctly (Excellent 144°, Good 108°, Acceptable 72°, Reject 36°; verify sum = 360°); states pie chart is appropriate because data represents proportions of a total (120 components); justification links discrete proportion-of-whole nature of data to pie chart's purpose.
Secure: Calculates at least three angles correctly; correct choice of pie chart with partial justification.
Developing: Uses correct formula for at least one angle; choice of graph stated without clear justification.
Emerging: Identifies the formula (frequency/total × 360°) or names a relevant graph type.

practice_questions.text: An engineer records the output temperature of a furnace every 30 minutes over a 4-hour heating cycle. Describe what type of graph should be used to display this data and explain why it is more suitable than a bar chart.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States line graph; explains that temperature is a continuous variable measured over time; a line graph shows how one continuous variable changes in response to another; a bar chart would imply the data is discrete/categorical, which is inappropriate for a time-series reading from a furnace.
Secure: States line graph; gives two developed reasons linking continuous/time-based data to the choice.
Developing: States line graph with one reason (e.g. 'shows change over time').
Emerging: Identifies that time-series data needs a graph but cannot specify which type.

practice_questions.text: A production record shows the number of components manufactured by four machines during one shift: Machine A = 320, Machine B = 280, Machine C = 150, Machine D = 250. Identify the most appropriate graph type for comparing these figures and give one reason why a histogram would be inappropriate.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Bar chart is most appropriate — data consists of discrete, named categories (four separate machines).
1 mark: A histogram is inappropriate because the data is not continuous or grouped into class intervals — the machines are separate categories, not a continuous variable.

practice_questions.text: A histogram shows the distribution of the lengths (in mm) of 100 machined shafts. The class intervals are all 2 mm wide. The class 148–150 mm has a bar height of 35; the class 150–152 mm has a bar height of 55; the class 152–154 mm has a bar height of 10. Calculate the total number of shafts that were within the specification range of 148–152 mm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Reads 35 + 55 = 90 shafts from the two bars covering 148–152 mm. Notes that 90 out of 100 = 90% within specification. Method clearly shown.
Secure: Correctly adds the two bar heights to 90 but does not convert to a percentage.
Developing: Identifies that the 148–150 and 150–152 bars must be included but makes an arithmetic error.
Emerging: Attempts to read values from the histogram with partial success.

practice_questions.text: Name the key visual difference between a bar chart and a histogram.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: In a histogram the bars touch (continuous data); in a bar chart the bars do not touch (discrete data). Accept either the touching/not-touching distinction or the continuous/discrete distinction.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturing company analyses its total production costs for a year: materials £48 000, labour £36 000, energy £12 000, overheads £24 000. Discuss whether a pie chart or a line graph would be better for presenting this data to company managers at a board meeting. Include a calculation to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculates total (£120 000) and at least one sector angle (e.g. materials = 48/120 × 360 = 144°); argues that a pie chart is better for this purpose because it immediately shows the relative proportions of each cost category and managers can see at a glance which cost dominates; notes that a line graph would only be appropriate if data changed over time — static annual totals are not time-series data; may note bar chart as a valid alternative to pie chart for comparison of absolute values; conclusion justified and linked to the audience (board meeting requires quick visual impact).
Secure: Correct choice and justification for pie chart with calculation of at least one angle; acknowledges why line graph is unsuitable.
Developing: Identifies pie chart as appropriate with partial justification; limited or missing calculation.
Emerging: Names a graph type and provides one reason.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'toughness'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: ability to absorb energy and resist fracture/cracking under impact. Accept equivalent wording focusing on impact resistance and not fracturing.

practice_questions.text: Give two physical properties that would be important when selecting a material for a bicycle frame. For each property, give one reason why it is needed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per property + reason pair (max 2 marks). Accept any two from: tensile strength (resists pulling forces from pedalling / rider weight); toughness (absorbs impact without fracturing); corrosion resistance (used outdoors in wet conditions); low density (not a physical property in the same list — do not award for density alone, but award if framed as 'light material needed for easy acceleration'). Two clear property + reason pairs required.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between malleability and ductility.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clearly distinguishes both terms with accurate definitions and links each to a manufacturing process (e.g. malleability — shaped by compression/rolling/hammering; ductility — drawn into wire/rod). Secure: Defines both terms accurately but without naming a specific process. Developing: Defines one term correctly. Emerging: Attempts a description but conflates the two terms.

practice_questions.text: A home security alarm is fitted on the outside wall of a house. Explain why corrosion resistance and resistance to environmental degradation are both important properties for the alarm housing.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains both properties with clear cause-and-effect reasoning — e.g. corrosion resistance prevents chemical reaction with rain/moisture that would weaken or damage the housing; environmental degradation resistance (e.g. UV light from sunlight breaking down the plastic) prevents the housing becoming brittle or discoloured over time. Distinguishes between the two properties. Secure: Explains both properties but the distinction between chemical corrosion and broader environmental degradation is not fully drawn. Developing: Explains one property correctly with a reason. Emerging: Names properties without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is choosing between mild steel and aluminium alloy for a children's climbing frame. Explain which material would be more suitable, referring to at least two physical properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Compares both materials across at least two relevant properties (e.g. corrosion resistance — aluminium forms a protective oxide layer, mild steel corrodes without treatment; toughness — both can be tough but steel is generally tougher; weight/density — aluminium is lighter, which reduces foundation load and is safer in the event of tipping). Makes a justified choice of material with clear engineering reasoning. Secure: Discusses two properties and makes a choice, but the reasoning for one property is less developed. Developing: Mentions two properties but treats them as advantages without comparing materials. Emerging: Makes a choice without property-based justification.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the physical properties required for the screen material of a modern mobile phone. In your answer, consider both the properties needed and the limitations of any material chosen.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies multiple relevant properties (hardness to resist scratching; toughness to survive drops without shattering; optical transparency; electrical insulation for safe handling; low thermal conductivity to avoid heat discomfort). Discusses at least one limitation or trade-off (e.g. increasing hardness through tempering or special formulation can reduce toughness; thicker glass improves toughness but adds weight). Reaches a justified conclusion about how engineers balance competing demands. Secure: Identifies three or more properties with explanation, makes one trade-off point, reaches a conclusion. Developing: Identifies two properties with some explanation; no trade-off discussed. Emerging: Names one or two properties without developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'hazard' in a workshop context.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: anything with the potential to cause harm. Accept equivalent wording (something that could cause injury or harm). Do not accept 'risk' conflated with hazard.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of engineering controls that could be used to reduce the risk of injury when operating a pillar drill.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each (max 2) for any two from: machine guard fitted over the rotating bit; interlock preventing the machine starting with the guard open; clamp or vice holding the workpiece securely; extraction system removing swarf. Do not accept PPE (goggles) as an engineering control.

practice_questions.text: Describe the three stages of a risk assessment.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes all three stages clearly — (1) identify the hazards present; (2) assess the risk (evaluate likelihood and severity of harm for each hazard); (3) decide and implement appropriate control measures. Secure: Describes all three stages but may not mention likelihood and severity in stage 2. Developing: Describes two stages correctly. Emerging: Identifies hazards and control measures but misses the risk evaluation stage.

practice_questions.text: Explain why PPE is described as the 'last resort' in the hierarchy of control measures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that PPE only protects the individual wearing it; it does not reduce or eliminate the hazard itself; it relies on the person wearing it correctly every time, which is less reliable than a physical barrier; higher-level controls such as machine guards reduce the hazard at source for everyone in the area, not just the PPE wearer. Secure: Explains that PPE relies on human behaviour and does not address the hazard; contrasts with engineering controls. Developing: States that PPE relies on the wearer but does not explain why higher-level controls are preferred. Emerging: States PPE is least effective without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A student is about to use a centre lathe for the first time. Explain the health and safety checks and precautions they should take before switching the machine on.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains at least four checks/precautions with reasons: check the workpiece is securely clamped in the chuck (loose workpiece will be thrown off at high speed); ensure the chuck guard is in the correct position (prevents contact with rotating chuck); tie back hair and remove jewellery / do not wear gloves (entanglement risk with rotating parts); check the area is clear of other people (injury to bystanders); wear safety goggles (swarf and chip hazard). Secure: Identifies three checks with reasons. Developing: Identifies two checks without full reasoning. Emerging: Identifies one check or gives generic safety points without lathe-specific detail.

practice_questions.text: A workshop supervisor has identified that students are at risk of eye injuries from metal swarf when filing. Using the hierarchy of control measures, discuss the range of controls that could be put in place, from most effective to least effective.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Works through the hierarchy systematically: Elimination — consider whether filing can be replaced by a process that produces less swarf (not always practical); Substitution — use a smoother file grade or a different process (limited effect on swarf); Engineering controls — fit an extraction hood over the filing area, use a vice to secure the workpiece (reduces swarf projection); Administrative controls — create a safe working procedure requiring goggles to be worn, train students on safe filing technique, mark a safe distance for bystanders; PPE — issue safety goggles as the last line of protection. Explains why higher levels are preferred and why PPE alone is insufficient. Reaches a conclusion. Secure: Covers all five levels; reasoning is present but one level lacks development. Developing: Covers three levels with some reasoning. Emerging: Lists PPE and one or two other measures without using the hierarchy structure.

practice_questions.text: Name one destructive test used to measure the tensile strength of a material.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: tensile test / tensile strength test. Accept equivalent naming.

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of non-destructive testing over destructive testing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each (max 2 marks) for any two from: the part/sample remains intact after testing; can be used on parts that are already in service / installed; allows 100% inspection of a production run without losing product; can test finished, assembled products. Do not accept vague answers like 'it is better'.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a Charpy impact test is carried out and what the result tells an engineer about the material.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes the notched sample being struck by a swinging pendulum; the height the pendulum reaches after impact is measured; a higher follow-through swing means less energy was absorbed, so the material is less tough. Secure: Describes the pendulum striking a sample and measuring energy absorbed; may not mention the notch or the follow-through height clearly. Developing: States that it tests toughness and involves striking with a pendulum, but lacks detail of the energy measurement. Emerging: Names the test without describing the method.

practice_questions.text: A quality control engineer receives a new batch of mild steel sheets from a supplier. Explain why a tensile test would be used rather than an ultrasonic inspection to check the material properties of the batch.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that tensile testing directly measures tensile strength (the mechanical property needed for quality control); the batch sample is sacrificed but this is acceptable as it is a small sample from the batch, not the product itself; ultrasonic inspection detects internal flaws/cracks in completed parts but does not measure tensile strength. Secure: Explains that tensile testing measures strength directly and gives quantified results; notes that a sample can be taken from the batch for destruction. Developing: States that tensile testing is appropriate for measuring strength but does not explain why NDT would be unsuitable or why the sample can be sacrificed. Emerging: Names tensile testing without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why non-destructive testing is essential for checking the welds on a suspension bridge cable after the bridge has been built and opened.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that the cable cannot be removed from the bridge or destroyed because it is a structural component carrying load; NDT (e.g. ultrasonic testing) can detect internal cracks or voids in the weld without cutting the cable or taking it out of service; the bridge remains safe and open during inspection. Secure: Explains that the cable must remain in place and NDT allows inspection without damage; may not explain the consequence of using DT. Developing: States that NDT does not damage the part but does not explain why damaging the cable would be unacceptable. Emerging: Names NDT without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and limitations of destructive testing when used to ensure the quality of engineering products leaving a factory. In your answer, refer to specific tests.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Discusses DT advantages (precise measurements of properties such as tensile strength via tensile test, toughness via impact test; gives quantified data for quality approval; methods are well-established). Discusses limitations (sample is destroyed so cannot go into service; cannot test every unit in a production run, only samples; cannot be used on in-service parts; selection of samples introduces statistical uncertainty). Refers to at least two specific tests by name. Reaches a conclusion on how DT and NDT are used together. Secure: Discusses advantages and one limitation with specific test named; conclusion present. Developing: Identifies advantages and one limitation; one specific test named. Emerging: Makes general points without referring to specific tests or drawing a reasoned conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
State the type of line used for each of the following on an engineering drawing:
(a) The visible outline of a component.
(b) A drilled hole that cannot be seen from the viewing direction.
(c) The axis of a cylindrical shaft.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each:
(a) Continuous thick line.
(b) Thin dashed line (hidden detail).
(c) Thin chain line (long-dash short-dash / centre line).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between third-angle orthographic projection and first-angle orthographic projection, and state which system this course requires.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that both show three views (front, plan, end); in third-angle, the plan sits above the front view and the right-side view sits to the right of the front view; in first-angle, views are placed on the opposite sides (plan below, right-side view to the left); third-angle is the system this course requires; identifies the truncated-cone symbol difference between the two. All four marks achievable.
Secure: Correctly identifies third-angle as the required system and at least two features of how view positions differ between the two systems.
Developing: Correctly names third-angle as the required system with one feature of view placement.
Emerging: States that third-angle is the required system.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a sectional view in engineering drawing, and explain why a sectional view is more useful than dashed hidden-detail lines for showing internal features of a complex component.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines sectional view (imagined cut through object along a cutting plane; internal shape revealed); describes thick chain cutting plane line with arrows and letter labels; hatching at 45° on cut surfaces; explains that for complex internal features (multiple bores, threads, recesses) many overlapping dashed lines would become difficult to read, whereas the section shows each internal feature as a clear outline.
Secure: Correct definition and at least two developed points on appearance and advantage.
Developing: Describes cutting through the object and mentions hatching, with one benefit stated.
Emerging: States that a sectional view shows the inside of the object.

practice_questions.text: Name the symbol used to identify third-angle projection on an engineering drawing and describe what it looks like.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Names the symbol (third-angle projection symbol / truncated cone symbol).
1 mark: Describes its appearance — a truncated cone shown in side elevation with the smaller circular end on the right (and the full diameter circle on the left).

practice_questions.text: A student draws an orthographic view of a cylindrical block. They draw a circle in the front view and a rectangle in the plan view. Explain why the plan view also needs a centre line passing through the centre of the rectangle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the cylinder is symmetrical about its axis; the centre line (thin chain line) marks the axis of symmetry and the centreline of the circular cross-section; without it, the drawing does not convey that the rectangular plan view represents a cylinder rather than a rectangular prism; the centre line also helps locate the centre for dimensioning the diameter.
Secure: States that centre lines mark the axis of a circular feature and explains why it is needed for the cylindrical block.
Developing: States that circles/cylinders need a centre line but does not fully develop the reason.
Emerging: Names the centre line as a requirement.

practice_questions.text: A mechanical engineer is producing a detailed drawing of a housing with several internal bores and recesses. Discuss the advantages and limitations of using sectional views compared with showing all internal features as dashed lines on the external views.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantage of sections — internal features shown as clear solid outlines with hatching, much easier to read than multiple overlapping dashed lines on external views; scale of internal features is immediately clear; a sectional view can be dimensioned without cluttering the external view. Limitation — the drawing sheet becomes more complex with additional views; the cutting plane position must be carefully chosen so it passes through all relevant features; if the part has many cuts in different planes, multiple sections may be needed adding to drawing time. Conclusion: for a complex multi-bore housing, sectional views significantly outweigh their drawbacks because clarity is critical for accurate machining. Sustained and developed argument throughout.
Secure: At least two advantages and one limitation, both developed, with a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One advantage and one limitation with some development.
Emerging: States one advantage of sectional views.
